answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, any delivery disruption from switching primary vendors (onboarding, ramp-up, unproven reliability under stress) carries outsized risk despite the low-cost vendor's quote meeting the 18% mandate on paper. memory_c2's positive switch experience was a single case and doesn't speak to performance under supply constraint. In contrast, memory_c4 and memory_c6 show the incumbent has previously yielded real margin and cost reductions through renegotiation and volume commitments without sacrificing service scope, and memory_c1 confirms the incumbent preserves integration stability. Given only one sourcing decision is available this cycle and the primary objective explicitly weights delivery risk alongside cost, the safer path is to renegotiate hard with the incumbent using the low-cost quote as leverage to try to meet the mandate while preserving continuity, deferring the switch-vendor option to next cycle pending more evidence on how it performs under tight capacity. I verified the switch-vendor and negotiate-terms source records since those are the two live contenders for this cycle's single decision slot.
